summary: Shanghai Jiao Tong University authors release SWE-Explore: 848 issues from SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and SWE-bench Multilingual, across 203 repositories and 10 languages, where an explorer must return five ranked line regions. Gold lines are the refined intersection of reads from at least two successful agent trajectories, then author-audited. On that target, general coding agents and most localizers sit far above BM25, TF-IDF and a static embedding retriever, but line-level recall for the general agents stays about 0.14-0.19. A restricted-context repair check on 150 instances ties several of those metrics to resolve rate, while perfect gold context still resolves only 59.7%.

claims.claim: Agentic explorers form a clear tier above classical retrieval on line-level exploration
claims.evidence: Table 6, all agents driven by GPT-5.4, K=5: HitRegion is 0.505-0.544 for OpenHands, Mini-SWE-Agent, AweAgent, Claude Code and Codex, versus BM25 0.065, TF-IDF 0.121 and Potion 0.069. Random is 0.003. The dense arm is a static word-embedding model (Potion), not a tuned code retriever. File hit rate for those agents is about 0.64-0.68, so about a third of gold files are still missed. No run-to-run interval.

claims.claim: Line-level coverage is the bottleneck, while file-level localization is already strong
claims.evidence: Table 6: general agents have HitFile 0.640-0.682 and nDCG@500 0.867-0.954, but line recall 0.140-0.194 and F1 0.182-0.223. CoSIL reaches line recall 0.788 and F1 0.602 with a worse noise-region rate (0.471 vs about 0.19-0.25). 'Already strong' overstates a file hit rate near two thirds. OrcaLoca, an academic localizer, has HitRegion 0.126.

claims.claim: The exploration metrics strongly track downstream repair
claims.evidence: Table 4: explorer-level Pearson r up to 0.950 (context efficiency) and Spearman up to 0.845 (recall@100), computed across the explorer pool, which includes Oracle and Random. That is a correlation over roughly fifteen systems, not over instances, and the two extremes inflate Pearson. Downstream resolve rates in Table 3 (n=150): Oracle 59.7%, CoSIL 59.3%, agents about 41-50%, TF-IDF 26.0%, RAG 23.3%, BM25 12.7%, Random 4.7%. The table caption says the patcher is GPT-5.4; the text says the rate is averaged over GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3-Pro.

claims.claim: Missing core context hurts repair more than redundant context, once enough evidence is present
claims.evidence: Figure 5, two stratified n=150 subsets, patchers GPT-5.4-mini and GPT-5.4. On the easier subset, resolve stays low until the visible fraction of gold regions jumps between 50% and 75%; extra random lines matter less after that, and hurt by 7-9 pp when no gold context is present. The harder subset barely moves. Oracle context itself resolves only 59.7% (Table 3), so exploration is not sufficient. An easier-subset dip from 0% to 25% gold context is flagged by the authors as possible memorization.

claims.claim: Changing the LLM shifts the operating point but does not remove the line-recall bottleneck
claims.evidence: Table 5, Mini-SWE-Agent only: GPT-5.4 line recall 0.154 and HitFile 0.655; GPT-5.4-mini recall 0.185; Sonnet-4.5 recall 0.118; Gemini-3-Pro recall 0.052 and HitFile 0.369. One run per model. These models also appear among the trajectory sources used to build the gold reads.

patterns.note: Under a fixed output (five ranked regions) and a fixed line budget, multi-step agents beat one-shot BM25, TF-IDF and Potion on hit rate, ranking and a downstream resolve check (Tables 3 and 6). The dense baseline is weak, gold lines are reads taken from successful agents including the same model families, and only issues those agents already solved are included. Line recall for general agents stays under 0.20.

Hiding repository lines outside the explorer's list changes resolve rate (Table 3, Figure 5), so what is read before patching matters. The task is issue repair, not discovery before a spec, people are not consulted, and full gold context still leaves about 40% of the n=150 subset unresolved.

One-shot BM25 and TF-IDF are near the floor on this line-level target (HitRegion 0.065 and 0.121) and resolve 12.7% and 26.0% when their five regions are the only context. That rejects lexical retrieval alone as an explorer. It does not test an agent that uses grep as a tool.

The Potion dense retriever matches BM25 (HitRegion 0.069; Table 3 RAG resolve 23.3%, below TF-IDF). A stronger code embedding model was not run, so this contradicts only this lightweight RAG setup, not embedding retrieval in general.

CoSIL, described as iterative code-graph search, has the highest non-oracle line recall (0.788) and matches Oracle resolve (59.3% vs 59.7%). The graph is not ablated against the same agent without it, and its noise-region rate is 0.471.

The paper adds a line-level exploration score on top of SWE-bench-family issues. The score's external check is one restricted-context protocol on 150 instances, with a caption/text disagreement about which patcher models were averaged.

methodology.sample: 848 instances, 203 repositories, 10 languages (Table 7: Python 547, Go 84, JavaScript 51, Rust 31, Java 30, others smaller). Kept only if at least two successful trajectories exist. Mean gold context 4.3 files, 4.7 regions, 1,578 lines. Downstream and degradation checks use n=150 subsets
methodology.baselines: Oracle (returns the gold regions), Random, BM25, TF-IDF, Potion RAG. Agents: Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands, Mini-SWE-Agent, AweAgent, AutoCodeRover, LocAgent, OrcaLoca, CoSIL. All scored at K=5
methodology.models: Table 6 agents use GPT-5.4. Table 5 swaps Mini-SWE-Agent across GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Kimi-K2.6, Sonnet-4.5, GLM-4.7, Gemini-3-Pro. Gold trajectories also come from GPT-5.4, Gemini-3-Pro, Sonnet-4.6, GLM-5.1 and Kimi-K2.6. Downstream patcher is Mini-SWE-Agent; caption and text disagree on whether results average GPT-5.4 with Gemini-3-Pro
methodology.variance: No seeds, no intervals, no significance tests on Tables 5-6. Correlations in Table 4 have no interval
methodology.ablations: Context-degradation sweep over the fraction of gold regions kept, with and without random padding (Figure 5). Appendix B defines pure-intersection and union label variants; the main tables use the refined core only. No ablation that holds out the evaluated model's own trajectories from the gold set
methodology.contamination_controls: Issues are public SWE-bench variants. §4.4 notes an easier-subset dip consistent with memorization when context is empty. No decontamination of gold or test instances. Gold reads are taken from the same strong models later used as explorers, and the paper does not say those evaluation runs were excluded from label construction
methodology.languages: Ten languages; Python is 64.5%. Java is 30 instances (3.5%)

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint. Comment says 20 pages, 5 figures. No journal_ref
standards.artifacts: Benchmark records, metric scripts and restricted-context scripts claimed at github.com/Qiushao-E/SWE-Explore-Bench and a Hugging Face dataset. Appendix G describes the release. Prompts for explorers are not printed in the paper

biases.detail: Instances need two successful agent solutions. Unsolved issues, which are where exploration failure matters most, are excluded. Limitations state this.

Gold lines are reads from successful runs of the same model families later scored as explorers. An agent can match the label by repeating its own earlier exploration. Public SWE-bench issues are also likely in training data; the empty-context dip is consistent with that.

The dense baseline is a static word embedding distilled from a sentence transformer. No contemporary code-embedding or reranker is included, so the 'retrieval fails' claim is strongest for BM25 and TF-IDF.
Gold context is what successful agents happened to read, not a proof that those lines are necessary or that other lines would not support a correct patch. The authors say so in the limitations.
An LLM promotes optional regions into the core, and the authors manually audit every promoted region. No agreement statistic is reported.
One run per explorer and per model. Table 4 correlations are over systems, not items.
K=5 was chosen because the refined gold set averages 4.7 regions. That couples the output budget to the label-construction choice.

coi.affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Xinjiang University; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign; three independent researchers
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code and Codex are among the explorers, alongside academic agents. No author affiliation with those vendors is stated
coi.detail: Academic benchmark. Commercial agents are scored, not promoted; they land in the same band as the open general agents.

verdict_reason: The benchmark asks a question the team actually has, and the gap from BM25 and TF-IDF to a multi-step agent is large on both the line metrics and the restricted-context repair check. The gold labels are reads from successful runs of the same model families, only already-solved issues are kept, the dense baseline is weak, correlations are over a handful of systems, and even the oracle context resolves 59.7% of the downstream subset. Use the relative ordering, not the absolute hit rates.
applicability: For issue-driven exploration before an edit, a one-shot lexical or lightweight embedding search is not a substitute for an agent that reads and follows calls: on this set those retrievers resolve 13-26% when their five regions are the only context, against about 41-50% for general agents. The agents still miss most of the gold lines (recall about 0.15), and Java is only 30 of 848 instances, so do not treat file-hit rates near 0.65 as good enough for a multi-repo Java change. Ask the explorer for line spans, not file names, and expect a graph-style search to raise recall while adding noise (CoSIL). Because labels are 'what a successful agent read' on issues agents already solved, a failure to match them is not proof the agent cannot fix the team's unsolved ingestion bugs. Keep tests and other repositories visible: the study is single-snapshot and single-repo.

conflicts_with.detail: There, a vector-retrieval ReAct agent beat a planner that delegated grep and file reads to a sub-agent on SWE-QA for every model tested (pooled pass 65.2% vs 46.2%), with many losses at the hand-off. Here, multi-step agents beat one-shot BM25, TF-IDF and a static embedding index on line-level exploration and downstream repair. The tasks differ (answer grading versus ranked regions for repair), and the retrieval systems are not the same.
